entries.meaning: A groan of frustration or defeat, aimed at a situation that has gone wrong rather than at a person. Extra letters in writing mean a longer, louder groan.
examples: "Argh! I just lost an hour of work."
Argh — the store closes in five minutes and I'm still ten minutes away.
He looked at the flat tire and let out a long argh.
"Aaargh. Why does this printer hate me?"
Argh, I knew I should have left earlier.
entries.русский: аргх / а-а-а — стон досады и бессилия, когда всё пошло не так

entries.meaning: A short, sharp bark of irritation, quicker and more sudden than ugh. It usually escapes before you have found words for whatever is annoying you.
examples: "Gah! This zipper is stuck again."
Gah, I hate group projects.
She opened an inbox full of spam and muttered a quiet gah.
"Gah! I said the wrong name in the meeting."
Gah — do not talk to me before coffee.
entries.русский: а-а! / тьфу ты — короткий резкий возглас раздражения, вырывается прежде слов

entries.ipa: no standard IPA — a growl with no vowel of its own: the r is held and carries the whole syllable, roughly /ɡr̩ː/
entries.respell: GRR (a low animal growl, teeth together, r drawn out)
entries.meaning: An imitation of an animal growl used to show annoyance, most often in writing or in a half-joking tone. Said out loud it is usually playful rather than genuinely angry.
examples: "Grr. The website logged me out again."
She texted back a single grr and a photo of the parking ticket.
Grrr — somebody took my lunch out of the fridge.
"Grr!" he said, wrestling with the jar lid.
Grr, I have to redo the whole slide deck.
entries.русский: р-р-р — рычание в знак досады, чаще в переписке и полушутя

entries.ipa: no standard IPA — a hum with the lips shut, pushed out through the nose and cut off, roughly /hm̩f/
entries.respell: HMF (mouth never opens; the sound is all nose and breath)
entries.meaning: A short snort through the nose that signals offended disapproval or grudging skepticism. It tells everyone you are unimpressed and a little insulted without committing you to words. The spelled-out harrumph is the one form that has a real vowel: /həˈrʌmf/.
examples: "Hmph. I wasn't even invited."
She crossed her arms and gave a loud hmph.
Hmph — that is not what he told me yesterday.
"Humph! Fine, do it your way."
He listened to the excuse, said hmph, and walked out.
entries.русский: хмф / пф — обиженное фырканье носом: не впечатлён и слегка задет

entries.meaning: The all-purpose groan of disgust, weariness, or annoyance. It covers a bad smell, a tedious chore, and news you did not want to hear, and it is one of the most common interjections in American speech.
examples: "Ugh, Monday already."
Ugh — the milk went bad.
"Traffic on the bridge is stopped." "Ugh."
She read the group chat and typed ugh before she typed anything else.
Ughhh, I have three more hours of this.
entries.русский: фу / у-у — стон отвращения, усталости или досады

entries.meaning: A blasphemous exclamation of exasperation, said when a person or a situation has pushed you past patience. This is real profanity, not a soft oath: it is a step stronger than jeez, which is its minced form, and a religious listener hears it as breaking a commandment rather than as ordinary swearing.
examples: "Christ, would you slow down?"
Christ — how many times do I have to explain this?
He looked at the repair bill and said, "Oh, Christ."
"Christ almighty, the meeting is three hours long."
Christ, I just mopped that floor.
entries.русский: Господи! / Боже мой! — богохульный возглас раздражения, груб.

entries.meaning: A mild swear for something that has just gone wrong, and a family-safe stand-in for shit. Most Americans hear it as mild, but it is still a swear word: keep it away from clients, strangers, and other people's children.
examples: "Crap, I left my badge at home."
Crap — the game went to overtime and I have to leave.
He dropped the tray and said crap under his breath.
"Crap! That's the second flat tire this month."
Crap, I forgot to hit send.
entries.русский: блин! / чёрт! — лёгкое ругательство при неудаче, приличная замена shit (разг.)

entries.meaning: The most common mild curse in American speech, used when something disappoints or irritates you. Said flat and clipped it is pure frustration; drawn out with a rising tone it flips to admiration, as in "Damn, that's good." It is mild to most ears and still a genuine curse to religious ones, who hear the original wish for damnation in it.
examples: "Damn, the flight got canceled."
Damn — I meant to pick that up on the way home.
He read the rejection letter and muttered damn.
"Damn! I hit reply-all again."
Damn, this line hasn't moved in ten minutes.
entries.русский: чёрт! / проклятье — самое частое лёгкое американское ругательство досады (разг.)

entries.meaning: A sharper, more directed damn, aimed at a situation that keeps going wrong. It is said as one word with no pause, which is why dammit is the ordinary written spelling.
examples: "Damn it, the file didn't save."
Dammit — I told you to check the oil.
He slammed the drawer shut. "Damn it all."
"Answer the phone, damn it."
Dammit, I was two minutes from finishing.
entries.русский: чёрт возьми! / да чёрт побери — резче damn, направлено на ситуацию

entries.meaning: A curse aimed at a person rather than at a situation — literally a wish for their damnation, which is why it still lands harder than damn it even when it is half a joke. In the third person (damn him, damn them) it is a complaint about somebody who is not in the room.
examples: "Damn you, you knew and you let me walk in there anyway."
Damn him — he borrowed the good ladder again and didn't bring it back.
"You were right." "Damn you. I hate it when you're right."
She read the letter a second time and said it quietly. "Damn you."
Damn them all, I am not paying a forty-dollar change fee.
entries.русский: будь ты проклят! / чтоб тебя — проклятие в адрес человека, а не ситуации
entries.variants: damn him, damn her, damn them all
entries.see also: damn it, go to hell, screw you

entries.meaning: A hostile dismissal telling someone they are finished as far as you are concerned. Unlike screw you, which friends trade as a joke, this one is almost always meant, and it is the line people remember years later.
examples: "Go to hell. I am not apologizing for something I didn't do."
"He wants us to eat the shipping cost." "Tell him to go to hell."
Go straight to hell — you promised me that was over.
She hung up, looked at the phone, and said, "Go to hell."
The hell with you, then. I'll move it myself.
entries.русский: иди к чёрту! / катись к чёрту — враждебный посыл, почти всегда всерьёз
entries.variants: go straight to hell, the hell with you, tell him to go to hell
entries.see also: screw you, damn you, to hell with it

entries.meaning: An exasperated appeal used when someone is wearing your patience thin. In this angry sense it is flat and clipped, unlike the drawn-out oh God of shock or dread. Most Americans treat it as mild; devout listeners do not, and to them it is the commandment about taking the name in vain.
examples: "God, you are impossible."
God — just pick a restaurant already.
"Oh God, not this argument again."
She rubbed her eyes. "God almighty, it's only Tuesday."
God, I wish this elevator would hurry up.
entries.русский: Господи! / Боже мой! — раздражённый возглас; верующие слышат имя всуе
entries.variants: oh God, my God, God almighty

entries.meaning: The strongest member of the damn family, adding blasphemy to the curse. It signals real anger, it is fully taboo at work, in front of children, and around anyone you have just met, and religious listeners object to it twice over.
examples: "Goddamn it, I asked for this yesterday."
Goddammit — the power went out right before I saved.
He kicked the bumper. "God damn it."
"Would you listen to me, goddamn it?"
Goddamn it, that's the third time this week.
entries.русский: да чтоб оно всё! / чёрт бы всё побрал — сильнейшее в семье damn, груб.
entries.see also: damn it, gosh darn it, dagnabbit

entries.meaning: A mild swear used alone for resigned annoyance, and used inside questions as an intensifier that sharpens the whole sentence (where the hell, why the hell). Alone it is milder than damn it; inside a question it is noticeably hotter. It is common enough to pass unnoticed among friends and still counts as swearing in a classroom or a client meeting.
examples: "Hell, I don't know why the server keeps crashing."
Where the hell did I put my keys?
"Hell — I might as well start over."
Why the hell would he say that to her?
Hell, at this point just cancel the whole thing.
entries.русский: чёрт! — само по себе лёгкая досада; внутри вопроса усилитель: какого чёрта
entries.see also: what the hell, heck, oh hell

entries.meaning: An exasperated blasphemous exclamation, usually aimed at a person who has just done something careless or maddening. Jesus Christ is the fuller and angrier form. Both are moderate as swearing and strong as blasphemy, so the room, not the word, decides how badly it lands.
examples: "Jesus, watch where you're going."
Jesus Christ — who parked like that?
He saw the estimate and said, "Jesus."
"Jesus H. Christ, would you two stop?"
Jesus, I've told him four times.
entries.русский: Господи Иисусе! / Боже мой — раздражённый богохульный возглас, груб.
entries.variants: Jesus Christ, Jesus H. Christ, oh Jesus

entries.meaning: Crap with the sinking realization built into it: you have just noticed the problem, and it is yours. It leans more toward dismay than toward anger.
examples: "Oh crap, I double-booked myself."
Oh crap — the dog got into the trash.
She checked the clock. "Oh, crap. I'm late."
"Oh crap! I sent that to the wrong Sarah."
Oh crap, the tickets were for last night.
entries.русский: ой, блин! / вот чёрт — досада в момент, когда понял, что влип

entries.meaning: A groan of dismayed frustration at bad news or an unwelcome sight. The longer oh hell no is a separate and very emphatic refusal.
examples: "Oh hell, the basement is flooded."
Oh hell — he brought his brother with him.
"Aw hell, I left the tickets on the counter."
She saw the check engine light come on. "Oh hell."
"They want us there at five in the morning." "Oh hell no."
entries.русский: ох, чёрт! / да чёрт возьми — стон досады при плохой новости
entries.see also: oh crap, hell, to hell with it

entries.meaning: A declaration that you are giving up on something out of frustration and moving on — the printable form of fuck it. Screw this aims the same feeling at the situation you are stuck in right now.
examples: "Screw it, I'm ordering pizza."
Screw this — I've been on hold for forty minutes.
He looked at the instructions, then at the pile of parts. "Screw it."
"Screw it, we'll fix it in the next release."
Screw that, I'm not driving four hours for a one-hour meeting.
entries.русский: да ну его! / плевать — бросить дело от досады; приличная замена fuck it
entries.see also: to hell with it, whatever, fine

entries.meaning: A hostile insult aimed straight at a person, and the softened form of fuck you. Softened is relative: it still ends conversations and starts arguments. Close friends sometimes use it jokingly, but never assume that.
examples: "Screw you, I did all the work on that."
Screw you — you knew and you didn't say anything.
"You're being dramatic." "Screw you."
He told his brother screw you and hung up.
"Screw him, we'll find another contractor."
entries.русский: да пошёл ты! / иди ты — смягчённое fuck you, но всё равно оскорбление
entries.variants: screw him, screw them, screw off
entries.see also: go to hell, shut up, whatever

entries.meaning: The strongest of the everyday one-word swears of frustration, and genuinely taboo in public, professional, and family settings. Shoot, sugar, and crap are the polite substitutes built from it.
examples: "Shit, I locked my keys in the car."
Shit — that's a police car behind us.
He read the number on the screen and said shit very quietly.
"Oh shit, the deadline was yesterday."
Shit, I think I deleted the wrong folder.
entries.русский: вот дерьмо! / бля! — сильное обиходное ругательство досады, груб., табу при чужих

entries.meaning: A more emphatic screw it: you are abandoning the effort out of anger or exhaustion. It can also be pointed at a person or a rule you have decided to stop respecting.
examples: "To hell with it, I'm going home."
The hell with it — I'll just buy a new one.
She stared at the spreadsheet another minute, then said, "To hell with it."
"To hell with this, the line isn't moving."
To hell with it, let's just tell them the truth.
entries.русский: да ну его к чёрту! / чёрт с ним — бросить дело от злости или усталости
entries.variants: the hell with it, to hell with this
entries.see also: screw it, fine, that does it

entries.meaning: Two distinct uses. 1. An angry or bewildered demand for an explanation, with the stress on hell. 2. Said flat, with a shrug, a decision to take the risk anyway — roughly "why not."
examples: "What the hell were you thinking?"
What the hell — my car was right here an hour ago.
"What the hell is that noise?"
He opened the box. "What the hell? These are the wrong size."
"Should we split the last piece?" "Ah, what the hell — take it."
It's my birthday, so what the hell, I'm getting the expensive one.
entries.русский: какого чёрта? — гневный вопрос; 2. сказанное ровно — «а, была не была»
entries.see also: what the heck, hell, are you kidding me

entries.meaning: A deliberately silly stand-in for Jesus Christ, built to match its rhythm and opening sounds. It is used to be funny about being annoyed rather than to hide real anger.
examples: "Cheese and crackers, look at this mess."
Cheese and crackers — who let the dog on the couch?
"Cheese and rice, that's expensive."
Grandma says cheese and crackers so she doesn't swear in front of the kids.
Cheese and crackers, I forgot the tickets again.
entries.русский: ёлки-палки! / ёшкин кот — нарочито дурашливая замена Jesus Christ
entries.variants: cheese and rice, oh cheese and crackers
entries.see also: jiminy Christmas, jeez Louise, mother of pearl

entries.meaning: An old-fashioned minced form of Christ, used for mild exasperation. It sounds gently folksy today and comes mostly from older speakers or from people reaching for a laugh.
examples: "Criminy, how much did they charge you?"
Criminy — that dog next door barks all night long.
"Criminy sakes, slow down."
He came in stamping the snow off his boots. "Criminy, it is cold out there."
Criminy, these instructions make no sense at all.
entries.русский: батюшки мои! / ёлки зелёные — устар., старомодная замена Christ

entries.meaning: A minced form of Christ, used for mild exasperation or startled annoyance. It peaked in mid-century American speech and now sounds like dialogue out of an old comic strip, which is mostly why people reach for it.
examples: "Cripes, would you look at this traffic."
Cripes — the dog just ate an entire stick of butter.
"Oh cripes, I left the water running upstairs."
He got the estimate back from the mechanic. "Cripes."
Hold still, for cripes' sake, I am almost done.
entries.русский: ёкарный бабай! / господи прости — устар., смягчённое Christ, как из старых комиксов
entries.variants: oh cripes, for cripes' sake, cripes almighty

entries.meaning: A soft substitute for crap, safe around children and coworkers. It marks small annoyances rather than real anger.
examples: "Crud, I forgot my lunch."
Crud — the pen leaked all over my bag.
"Oh, crud. The store already closed."
She caught a typo in the last line and said crud.
Crud, I think I left the light on in the garage.
entries.русский: блин! / ёлки — мягкая замена crap, годится при детях и коллегах

entries.meaning: A rural, old-fashioned scrambling of goddamn it, now heard mainly in cartoons, Westerns, and self-aware humor. Almost nobody says it with a straight face anymore.
examples: "Dagnabbit, the fence is down again."
Dagnabbit — those kids cut through my yard every morning.
"Dad gum it, where did I put my hat?"
He kicked the tire and hollered dagnabbit.
Dagnabbit, I can never get this lid off.
entries.русский: ах ты ж, едрёна корень! — устар., деревенская замена goddamn it, ныне только в шутку
entries.variants: dagnab it, dad gum it, dadgummit

entries.meaning: A soft, slightly Southern-flavored substitute for damn. Like the word it replaces, it works as a complaint when it is clipped and as admiration when it is drawn out.
examples: "Dang, that storm knocked the power out."
Dang it — I dropped my phone in the parking lot.
"Dang, this line is long."
He looked at the dent in the door. "Dang it all."
Dang, I meant to record that game.
entries.русский: блин! / ёлки-моталки — мягкая замена damn, с южным оттенком

entries.meaning: The standard polite replacement for damn, usable in front of anyone at all. Darn it is the full frustration form, while darn before a noun is just an intensifier for something that is annoying you.
examples: "Darn it, the batteries are dead."
Darn — I missed the turn.
"This darn printer jams every single time."
She dropped a stitch and said, "Darn it all."
Darn, I was hoping they'd still have my size.
entries.русский: блин! / ёлки-палки — приличная замена damn; перед существительным «дурацкий»
entries.variants: darn it, darn it all, dern
entries.see also: dang, damn it, gosh darn it

entries.meaning: A folksy minced oath for goddamn, used both as an exclamation and as a mild intensifier in front of a noun. It reads as small-town and gently old-fashioned.
examples: "Doggone it, the mower won't start."
Doggone — the deer got into the tomatoes again.
"Where is my doggone wrench?"
He shook his head slowly. "Doggone it all anyway."
Doggone it, I forgot to mail the check.
entries.русский: ёлки зелёные! — устар., простецкая замена goddamn; перед существительным «окаянный»

entries.meaning: A quaint, mild curse of annoyance, historically a squeezed-down "God rot it." It survives mostly in children's books and in playful speech.
examples: "Drat, the cookies burned."
Drat — I forgot my umbrella again.
"Drat it all, the cat got out."
She missed the bus by ten seconds. "Drat."
Drat, there goes my whole afternoon.
entries.русский: тьфу ты! / вот незадача — устар., книжн., милое ругательство из детских книжек

entries.meaning: The letter f said out loud in place of fuck — the most transparent minced oath in the language, since it names the first letter of the word it is dodging. It fills every slot the original does: eff it, effing, what the eff, and the hostile eff off.
examples: "Eff it, I'm taking the train."
What the eff — somebody parked across two spaces again.
This effing printer has been broken since March.
She caught herself in front of her mother-in-law and said eff instead.
"He told me to eff off," she said, still furious about it a week later.
entries.русский: эф / фиг — замена fuck по его первой букве, ср. русское «на букву…»
entries.variants: eff it, effing, what the eff, eff off

entries.meaning: A gentle exclamation of annoyance or dismissal, meaning roughly "how irritating" or "nonsense." It is strongly old-fashioned and usually said with a wink.
examples: "Fiddlesticks, I've lost my reading glasses again."
Fiddlesticks — the recipe calls for buttermilk and I have none.
"You'll never finish in time." "Fiddlesticks. Watch me."
She looked at the broken zipper and said fiddlesticks.
Fiddlesticks, the bank closed ten minutes ago.
entries.русский: вздор! / чепуха — устар., мягкий возглас досады и отмахивания

entries.meaning: Not a standalone interjection but the intensifier that carries the anger inside other expressions — the minced substitute for fucking. It slots in before adjectives and nouns and inside fixed phrases like are you freaking kidding me.
examples: "Are you freaking kidding me?"
This freaking door sticks every time it rains.
"Freakin' unbelievable," he said, staring at the scoreboard.
I have been on hold for two freaking hours.
"Would you just open the frigging window?"
entries.русский: чёртов / грёбаный — смягчённая замена fucking; не самостоятельное междометие
entries.see also: eff, frick, are you kidding me

entries.meaning: A minced form of fuck, common with teenagers and with anyone trying to keep it clean. What the frick and frick it mirror the phrases it replaces, sound for sound.
examples: "Frick, I forgot my homework."
What the frick — who ate the last slice?
"Frick it, I'll just walk."
He stubbed his toe on the bed frame and yelled frick.
Are you frickin' serious right now?
entries.русский: блин! / фиг — смягчённое fuck, ходовое у подростков
entries.variants: frick it, what the frick, frickin'

entries.meaning: A candy-flavored substitute for fuck, chosen because it starts the same way. Saying it out loud usually announces that you are consciously not swearing, which is half the point of using it.
examples: "Fudge, I spilled coffee on my shirt."
Oh fudge — the recipe needed two eggs, not one.
"Fudge!" she said, catching herself in front of the kids.
He hit his thumb with the hammer. "Fudge."
Fudge, the meeting started five minutes ago.
entries.русский: блин! — «конфетная» замена fuck по первому звуку: слышно, что человек сдержался

entries.meaning: An exasperated reaction to something excessive, ridiculous, or exhausting. It is weary rather than hostile and is completely safe in mixed company.
examples: "Good grief, how much luggage did you bring?"
Good grief — this form is eleven pages long.
"Good grief. They raised the price again."
She saw the line stretching out the door. "Good grief, forget it."
Good grief, just let the man finish a sentence.
entries.русский: боже мой! / ну надо же — усталая досада от чего-то чрезмерного, вполне прилично
entries.see also: oh brother, sheesh, for crying out loud

entries.meaning: The everyday minced form of God, and the syllable that gosh darn it and for gosh sakes are built on. In this category it carries mild exasperation rather than shock, and it is safe in front of absolutely anyone.
examples: "Gosh, would you two give it a rest."
Gosh — that is the fourth time he has rescheduled on me.
"Oh gosh, I completely forgot to call the vet back."
She went through the receipts twice. "My gosh, where is it all going?"
Slow down, gosh, nobody is chasing you.
entries.русский: господи! / батюшки — приличная замена God, безопасна при ком угодно
entries.variants: oh gosh, my gosh, gosh no
entries.see also: gosh darn it, jeez, for God's sake

entries.meaning: A doubly minced goddamn it — gosh for God and darn for damn. It is the safest way to sound genuinely fed up in front of anyone.
examples: "Gosh darn it, the mower's out of gas."
Gosh darn it — I asked for no onions.
"Gosh dang it, that's the wrong screw again."
He fumbled the keys twice. "Gosh darn it all."
Gosh darn it, I left my wallet at the restaurant.
entries.русский: ах ты ж ёлки-палки! — вдвойне смягчённое goddamn it, предельно прилично
entries.variants: gosh darn, goshdarnit, gosh dang it, gol dang it

entries.meaning: A playful, letter-by-letter way of saying hell without saying it, named for the shape of the two l's. Adults use it to be funny in front of children, and children use it to get away with almost swearing.
examples: "What the H-E-double-hockey-sticks is going on in here?"
"H-E-double-hockey-sticks no — I am not sitting through that again."
"Where the H-E-double-hockey-sticks did I leave my glasses?"
"H-E-double-toothpicks, that hurt."
Mom never says the word, so we all grew up saying H-E-double-hockey-sticks.
entries.русский: детская побуквенная замена hell, ср. «слово на букву „а“»; аналога в русском нет

entries.meaning: The safe replacement for hell, and it fills exactly the same slots: alone for mild annoyance, and inside a question as an intensifier. It is mild enough for the office.
examples: "Heck, I've been trying to fix that for a week."
Where the heck is the remote?
"Oh heck — I left the oven on."
Why the heck would they schedule it that early?
"Heck no, I'm not driving in this."
entries.русский: чёрт побери (смягч.) — приличная замена hell; в вопросе усилитель: какого фига

entries.meaning: A wholesome minced form of Jesus, exasperated and a little startled at the same time. It is thoroughly mid-century and reads today as either grandparental or deliberately corny.
examples: "Jeepers, you scared the life out of me."
Jeepers creepers — who invited all these people?
"Oh jeepers, I think I just backed into the mailbox."
He looked at the tangle of extension cords under the desk. "Jeepers."
Jeepers, I was only trying to help.
entries.русский: батюшки светы! — устар., благонравная замена Jesus, звучит по-стариковски

entries.meaning: The everyday minced form of Jesus, used for exasperation or mild shock. It is safe in most casual settings, though a few very religious speakers still hear the original word inside it.
examples: "Jeez, give me a second."
Jeez — you scared me half to death.
"Geez, how much did that cost?"
He slammed the trunk shut. "Jeez, this thing weighs a ton."
Jeez, I already said I was sorry.
entries.русский: господи! / ё-моё — обиходная смягчённая замена Jesus (разг.)

entries.meaning: A rhyming, comic extension of jeez for when plain jeez is not enough. The rhyme keeps it exasperated but good-natured.
examples: "Jeez Louise, how long does it take to order a coffee?"
Geez Louise — forty dollars for parking?
"Jeez Louise, would you two stop bickering?"
She looked at the pile of laundry on the bed. "Jeez Louise."
Jeez Louise, I only asked a question.
entries.русский: ё-моё, ёлки-моталки! — шутливое рифмованное усиление jeez

entries.meaning: An old minced form of Jesus Christ that quietly keeps the initials. It is thoroughly wholesome and sounds like something a grandparent says.
examples: "Jiminy Christmas, look at the size of that bill."
Jiminy Christmas — the kids tracked mud through the whole house.
"Jiminy Cricket, you nearly gave me a heart attack."
He counted the receipts twice. "Jiminy Christmas."
Jiminy Christmas, would you please turn that down?
entries.русский: матушки мои! — устар., старая замена Jesus Christ, сохраняющая его инициалы

entries.meaning: A minced Jesus Christ that keeps the J, the rhythm, and the initials, and swaps in the disciple who betrayed him. It is old, faintly rural, and now better known as the name of a heavy metal band than as an oath.
examples: "Judas Priest, how long does it take to change one tire?"
Judas Priest — every light between here and the office was red.
"Judas, would you let me finish a sentence?"
He pulled the tarp back off the boat and stared. "Judas Priest."
Turn that down, Judas Priest, I can hear it from the driveway.
entries.русский: устар., замена Jesus Christ через имя Иуды — те же инициалы; аналога в русском нет
entries.variants: Judas, Judas H. Priest, sweet Judas Priest
entries.see also: jiminy Christmas, cheese and crackers, Christ

entries.meaning: A comic minced oath that swerves away from motherfucker after the first word. It is almost always said for the laugh rather than out of real fury.
examples: "Mother of pearl, that water is cold."
Sweet mother of pearl — who scheduled a meeting at seven in the morning?
"Mother of pearl! Would you look at this line?"
She read the repair quote and said mother of pearl.
I hit my head on that beam every single time. Mother of pearl.
entries.русский: мать честная! — комичный уход в сторону от motherfucker после первого слова
entries.see also: son of a biscuit, cheese and crackers, sugar

entries.meaning: A mild mid-century exclamation of disappointment or dismissal. Nuts to that means you refuse to bother with something at all.
examples: "Nuts, the machine took my dollar."
Aw, nuts — we're out of coffee filters.
"Nuts to that, I'm not waiting three hours."
He missed the shot and muttered nuts.
Nuts, I thought the game was tonight.
entries.русский: тьфу ты! / вот досада — устар., лёгкое разочарование; nuts to that — «да ну его»

entries.meaning: A dismissive noise of annoyance or contempt, meaning roughly "nonsense" or "forget it." It is soft, old-fashioned, and often used around children.
examples: "Phooey, the batteries died again."
Aw, phooey — the pool's closed for the season.
"They said it can't be done." "Phooey."
She spat out the cold coffee. "Phooey."
Phooey, I wanted the window seat.
entries.русский: тьфу! / фу — устар., пренебрежительный возглас: «ерунда», «да ну»

entries.meaning: A small, harmless groan of disappointment when a plan falls through. It is the sound of mild bad luck, not of real anger, and it is safe in front of anyone.
examples: "Rats, the store is out of them."
Rats — I just missed the train.
"Oh, rats. I wanted to see that movie."
He checked the empty mailbox again. "Rats."
Rats, my phone died in the middle of the call.
entries.русский: эх! / вот досада — безобидное огорчение, когда планы сорвались

entries.meaning: A nineteenth-century minced hell that survives only inside a question frame: what in Sam Hill, where in Sam Hill, and so on. Nobody says plain Sam Hill by itself, and the whole phrase now sounds like a Western.
examples: "What in Sam Hill is that supposed to mean?"
Where in Sam Hill did I put the truck keys?
"Who in Sam Hill told you that was a good idea?"
He stood looking at the hole in the fence. "What in Sam Hill happened here?"
How in Sam Hill are we supposed to fit all that in one load?
entries.русский: устар., замена hell только внутри вопроса: what in Sam Hill — «какого лешего»
entries.variants: what in Sam Hill, where in Sam Hill, who in Sam Hill

entries.meaning: An exasperated hiss at something excessive, unreasonable, or over the top. It often carries a note of "calm down" or "that is a lot."
examples: "Sheesh, I was only asking."
Sheesh — twelve dollars for a sandwich?
"Sheesh, take it easy on him."
She scrolled through the list of requirements. "Sheesh."
Sheesh, you'd think I asked him for a kidney.
entries.русский: ну ты даёшь! / фух — раздражённый выдох: «полегче», «это уже слишком»

entries.meaning: The polite stand-in for shit, especially common in the South and Midwest and safe almost anywhere. It marks a small mistake or an inconvenient discovery.
examples: "Shoot, I left my phone in the car."
Oh shoot — I forgot to call her back.
"Shoot, we're out of milk."
She saw that the meter had expired. "Aw, shoot."
Well, shoot. I guess we're doing it the hard way.
entries.русский: блин! / ёлки — приличная замена shit, частая на Юге и Среднем Западе

entries.meaning: A comic minced form of son of a bitch, usually aimed at a situation rather than a person. The joke is the swerve away from the real phrase at the last possible second.
examples: "Son of a biscuit, I locked myself out."
Son of a biscuit — the ladder just tipped over.
"Son of a biscuit eater, that's expensive."
He cracked his elbow on the doorframe. "Son of a biscuit!"
Son of a biscuit, the game got rained out again.
entries.русский: ёшкин кот! — комичный уход в сторону от son of a bitch в последний момент
entries.variants: son of a biscuit eater, son of a monkey
entries.see also: son of a gun, mother of pearl, cheese and crackers

entries.meaning: Two uses. 1. An exclamation of annoyance or grudging surprise at how something turned out. 2. Aimed at a person, a mild insult or a backhanded compliment, as in "you old son of a gun." Both senses now sound like your grandfather.
examples: "Son of a gun, the thing actually works."
Son of a gun — I've been looking for that wrench all week.
"Son of a gun! The engine quit on me again."
"You beat me by two strokes, you old son of a gun."
That son of a gun charged me twice for the same part.
Son of a gun, I thought we were finally done with this.
entries.русский: вот те на! — устар., досада или удивление; о человеке — «шельма, хитрец»
entries.see also: son of a biscuit, doggone, nuts

entries.meaning: A sweet substitute for shit, chosen for the shared first sound. It is strongly Southern and belongs to speakers who avoid swearing entirely; outside the South it can sound put on. The joke spelling sugar honey iced tea spells out the word it is dodging.
examples: "Sugar, I burned the biscuits."
Oh sugar — I forgot to defrost the chicken.
"Sugar!" she said, dropping the lid of the casserole dish.
He caught himself mid-word and finished with sugar.
Sugar, the sitter just canceled on us.
entries.русский: ой, блин! — диал. (южные штаты), «сладкая» замена shit по первому звуку
entries.variants: oh sugar, sugar honey iced tea

entries.meaning: A frontier-era minced damnation, almost always used inside what in tarnation. Like Sam Hill it survives mainly as costume — cartoons, Westerns, and people doing an impression of a cranky old farmer.
examples: "What in tarnation is going on out here?"
Tarnation — the raccoons got into the feed again.
"Who in tarnation parked in the middle of the road?"
He opened the bill for the new well pump. "Tarnation."
Get down off that roof, tarnation, before you break your neck.
entries.русский: какого лешего! — устар., замена damnation, почти только в what in tarnation
entries.variants: what in tarnation, who in tarnation, consarn it

entries.meaning: Two uses, exactly parallel to what the hell but clean. 1. A demand for an explanation. 2. With a shrug, a decision to go ahead and do the thing anyway.
examples: "What the heck happened to my sandwich?"
What the heck — the door was locked five minutes ago.
"What the heck is he doing up there?"
She opened the package. "What the heck? I ordered blue."
"Do you want dessert?" "What the heck, sure."
It's Friday, so what the heck, let's leave early.
entries.русский: какого фига? — приличный what the hell; ровным тоном — «а, была не была»
entries.variants: what the heck?, what in the heck

entries.meaning: A blasphemous plea for someone to stop being unreasonable. It is the sharpest member of the for ...'s sake family, and to a religious listener it is not exasperation but profanity.
examples: "For Christ's sake, just answer the question."
For Christ's sake — the meeting was supposed to start an hour ago.
"Pick up the phone, for Christ's sake."
He threw up his hands. "For Christ's sake, I already told you."
For Christ's sake, it isn't that complicated.
entries.русский: ради Христа! / да господи ж ты — самое резкое в этой группе, богохульно, груб.
entries.variants: for Christ sake, for Christ's sakes
entries.see also: for God's sake, Christ, for Pete's sake

entries.meaning: A wholesome expression of exasperation that stands in for the religious oaths it imitates. It is the safest way to announce to a room that you have had enough.
examples: "For crying out loud, shut the door."
For crying out loud — I've called three times already.
"It's the fourth reschedule, for crying out loud."
She dropped the folder twice in a row. "For crying out loud."
For crying out loud, would somebody answer that phone?
entries.русский: да сколько же можно! / ну ёлки-палки — вполне приличное «я дошёл до предела»
entries.see also: for Pete's sake, good grief, for heaven's sake

entries.meaning: An exasperated appeal, normally urging someone to act or to stop. It is mild for most listeners and moderately offensive to religious ones. For gosh sakes is the minced version and carries none of the offense.
examples: "For God's sake, be careful with that."
For God's sake — he's only eight years old.
"Let her finish, for God's sake."
He read the email twice. "For God's sake, that is not what I asked for."
For God's sake, put on a coat.
entries.русский: ради бога! / господи ты боже мой — раздражённый призыв сделать или прекратить
entries.variants: for God's sakes, for gosh sakes
entries.see also: for Christ's sake, for heaven's sake, for the love of God

entries.meaning: A gentle, church-safe version of for God's sake, common with older speakers and around children. It scolds without offending anyone.
examples: "For heaven's sake, wipe your feet."
For heaven's sake — the poor thing hasn't eaten all day.
"For heaven's sake, it's only a scratch."
She looked down the muddy hallway. "For heaven's sakes."
For heaven's sake, call your mother back.
entries.русский: ради всего святого! — мягкий, безобидный вариант for God's sake, часто у старших
entries.variants: for heaven's sakes, for the love of heaven
entries.see also: for God's sake, for Pete's sake, good grief

entries.meaning: A minced oath in which "Pete" quietly replaces a holy name. It is exasperated but never rude, which is why parents and teachers reach for it first.
examples: "For Pete's sake, hurry up."
For Pete's sake — the recycling goes in the blue bin.
"Just ask him, for Pete's sake."
He waited another ten minutes. "For Pete's sake, where is she?"
For Pete's sake, turn the music down.
entries.русский: ну ради бога же! / ёлки-палки — смягчённая клятва: «Пит» вместо святого имени
entries.variants: for Pete's sakes, for pity's sake
entries.see also: for crying out loud, for heaven's sake, for God's sake

entries.meaning: A pleading, dramatic version of for God's sake, used when you are begging someone to stop or to act. The Mike and Pete versions are the minced forms and are safe anywhere.
examples: "For the love of God, don't tell her I said that."
For the love of God — somebody turn off that alarm.
"For the love of Mike, just read the instructions."
She had been on hold for an hour. "For the love of God, pick up."
For the love of all that's holy, stop clicking that pen.
entries.русский: ради всего святого, умоляю! — мольба прекратить; варианты с Mike и Pete безобидны
entries.variants: for the love of Mike, for the love of Pete, for the love of all that's holy
entries.see also: for God's sake, for crying out loud, come on

entries.meaning: A warning to stop pushing — physically, or more often with questions, pressure, or criticism. It is more confrontational than cut it out because it treats the other person as a threat rather than as a nuisance.
examples: "Back off. I said I would handle it."
Back off — she has had a rough enough week already.
He was standing about six inches away, so I told him to back off.
The two of them squared up until the bartender said, "Back off, both of you."
Back off a little and let the kid figure it out himself.
entries.русский: отстань! / не наседай — предупреждение перестать давить, жёстче cut it out
entries.variants: back off!, back the heck off, back way off
entries.see also: knock it off, cut it out, give it a rest

entries.meaning: A protest that something is unfair, unreasonable, or obviously wrong. Stretched out with a falling pitch it means "you cannot be serious"; short and clipped it simply means "hurry up."
examples: "Come on, that was clearly a foul."
Oh come on — you promised you'd be there.
"C'mon, we're going to miss the previews."
He watched a third car cut him off. "Come on!"
Come on, nobody actually believes that.
entries.русский: да ладно! / да брось — протест против несправедливого; коротко — «давай быстрее»
entries.variants: c'mon, oh come on, aw come on
entries.see also: give me a break, oh please, seriously

entries.meaning: A direct order to stop an annoying behavior, most often aimed at children, siblings, or friends. It is firm without being hostile.
examples: "Cut it out, both of you."
Cut it out — I'm trying to listen.
"You keep kicking my seat. Cut it out."
She heard the giggling start up again. "Cut that out."
Cut it out, that stopped being funny an hour ago.
entries.русский: прекрати! / хватит — твёрдый, но не злой приказ прекратить надоедливое
entries.see also: knock it off, quit it, enough

entries.meaning: An order to stop talking about one particular thing. Where cut it out is about behavior, drop it is about a topic, and the sharpness usually means the topic hurts.
examples: "Drop it, Dad. I don't want to talk about it."
Just drop it — we are not relitigating the seating chart.
"So about the car—" "Drop it."
He kept circling back to it until she finally said, "Drop it. Please."
I asked him twice to drop it and he brought it up again at dinner.
entries.русский: хватит об этом! / оставь эту тему — приказ прекратить разговор, а не действие
entries.variants: just drop it, drop the subject, let it drop
entries.see also: cut it out, enough, knock it off

entries.meaning: A flat command to stop, said when patience has run out. It carries real authority and works from a parent, a teacher, or a manager without sounding coarse.
examples: "Enough. Go to your rooms."
Enough already — I have heard this story four times.
"That's enough, we are not discussing it any further."
The room kept arguing until she said, "Enough."
Enough, I don't want to hear another word about it.
entries.русский: хватит! / довольно — властное «всё, прекратили», уместно у родителя или начальника
entries.variants: enough already, that's enough, enough is enough
entries.see also: that does it, knock it off, cut it out

entries.meaning: A weary demand that somebody stop repeating something — a complaint, a joke, a piece of nagging. It is blunter than drop it and comes with an audible eye-roll.
examples: "Give it a rest, you've told that story three times tonight."
Give it a rest — nobody here cares who won in 2003.
"You could have taken the other exit." "Give it a rest."
He hummed the same eight bars for an hour before somebody said, "Give it a rest."
Would you give it a rest for five minutes so I can think?
entries.русский: да уймись уже! / хватит уже об этом — устало, с закатыванием глаз
entries.variants: just give it a rest, give that a rest
entries.see also: drop it, knock it off, enough

entries.meaning: An exasperated objection that something is unfair or that you are simply not buying it. Depending on the situation it means "stop bothering me" or "that excuse is ridiculous."
examples: "Give me a break, I've been here since six."
Gimme a break — he has never done a day of work on that project.
"Traffic again?" "Give me a break."
She read the fine print. "Give me a break, there's a fee for everything."
Give me a break, it's only my first week.
entries.русский: да ладно тебе! / не смеши — «это несправедливо» или «не поверю»
entries.see also: come on, oh please, are you kidding me

entries.meaning: A blunt order to stop, a notch harder than cut it out. It usually arrives after you have already asked politely once.
examples: "Knock it off before somebody gets hurt."
Knock it off — I can hear you two from downstairs.
"Hey. Knock it off."
The coach blew his whistle. "Knock it off, all of you."
Knock it off, I'm on the phone.
entries.русский: а ну прекрати! / завязывай — резче cut it out, после первой вежливой просьбы
entries.see also: cut it out, quit it, enough

entries.meaning: A short complaint telling someone to stop poking, teasing, or otherwise pestering you. It is the classic sibling protest and sounds young in an adult's mouth.
examples: "Quit it, you're getting sand everywhere."
Quit it — that's my chair.
"He keeps touching my stuff." "Quit it, Danny."
She swatted his hand away. "Quit that."
Quit it, I'm trying to concentrate.
entries.русский: отстань! / перестань — детское «не трогай», классический протест младшего в семье
entries.see also: cut it out, knock it off, shut up

entries.meaning: A rude command to stop talking. Said to a stranger, a coworker, or anyone with authority over you it is a genuine insult and can end the relationship; between close friends and siblings it can be a joking dismissal, and with a sharp rise in pitch it turns into "no way, really?"
examples: "Shut up and let her finish."
Shut up — I am not having this conversation again.
"You sing worse than I do." "Oh, shut up."
The two of them argued until their father yelled, "Shut up, both of you."
Shut up, I can't hear the announcement.
entries.русский: заткнись! / замолчи — груб.; между близкими бывает шуткой, с чужими — оскорбление
entries.see also: knock it off, cut it out, enough

entries.meaning: The announcement that your patience has just run out and you are about to do something about it. It is almost always followed by what that something is.
examples: "That does it, I'm calling the landlord."
That's it — everybody out of the pool.
"That does it. We're leaving."
The alarm went off a fourth time. "That tears it, I'm unplugging it."
That's it, I am never ordering from them again.
entries.русский: ну всё! / это последняя капля — терпение кончилось, сейчас последуют меры
entries.variants: that's it, that tears it, that's the last straw
entries.see also: enough, to hell with it, screw it

entries.meaning: An outraged question that expects no answer — you are protesting that something is absurd or unfair. The stress lands hard on kidding.
examples: "Are you kidding me? They canceled it again?"
Are you kidding — forty-five dollars for parking?
"The game's rained out." "Are you kidding me?"
She stared at the empty pan. "Are you serious? I left for one minute."
Are you kidding me, the deadline moved up a week?
entries.русский: ты шутишь?! / да ты издеваешься — возмущённый вопрос без ожидания ответа
entries.variants: are you kidding, are you serious, are you freaking kidding me
entries.see also: you gotta be kidding me, seriously, unbelievable

entries.meaning: Said alone with a sigh, a small expression of despairing exasperation at someone's behavior — roughly "I cannot believe you." It is mild enough for almost any setting, including the office.
examples: "Honestly. You'd lose your head if it weren't attached."
Honestly — I turn my back for one minute.
"He did it again." "Honestly!"
She picked the wet towel up off the bed. "Honestly, every single day."
Honestly, I don't know why I bother.
entries.русский: ну честное слово! / боже мой — усталый вздох досады: «ну как так можно»

entries.meaning: A weary eye-roll put into words, used when someone is being dramatic, ridiculous, or entirely predictable. It is dismissive but harmless.
examples: "Oh brother, here we go again."
Oh brother — he's telling the fishing story.
"She says the whole thing is my fault." "Oh brother."
He watched the fine print scroll past. "Oh, brother."
Oh brother, not another software update.
entries.русский: ну вот, опять! / господи — озвученное закатывание глаз, беззлобно

entries.meaning: A scornful rejection of what someone just said: you find it exaggerated, insincere, or ridiculous. The tone is flat and falling, nothing like the pleading please.
examples: "Oh please, you were nowhere near the finish line."
Oh please — he's been saying that for years.
"I would have won if the wind hadn't picked up." "Oh, please."
She rolled her eyes at the commercial. "Please. Nothing works that fast."
Oh please, like anybody's going to notice.
entries.русский: да брось! / ой, ну хватит — презрительное «не верю, это смешно»
entries.see also: come on, give me a break, whatever

entries.meaning: Said flat, a rebuke: you are pointing out that someone has just done something thoughtless. Said with a rising pitch the same word is ordinary surprise instead, so the tone carries the entire meaning.
examples: "Really. You parked across two spaces."
Really — you're going to eat that over my keyboard?
"I told her you said it." "Really? Thanks a lot."
He watched his roommate leave the dish in the sink. "Really, man?"
Really, after everything I did for him?
entries.русский: ну серьёзно? / вот как — ровным тоном упрёк; с повышением — обычное удивление

entries.meaning: An exasperated challenge meaning "you cannot possibly be doing this." Flat and falling it is a complaint; rising, it is disbelief.
examples: "Seriously? You ate the last one?"
Seriously — it has been down all morning.
"The meeting moved to five o'clock." "Seriously."
She found the printer jammed for the third time. "Seriously?"
Seriously, who leaves a shopping cart in the middle of the lot?
entries.русский: серьёзно?! / да ты что — раздражённый вызов «ты правда это делаешь?»
entries.see also: really, are you kidding me, unbelievable

entries.meaning: An outraged verdict on somebody's gall. It is said about the offender rather than to them, and it usually arrives about ten seconds after they have left the room.
examples: "The nerve. He asked me to cover his shift on my day off."
The nerve of some people — she took the spot I was clearly waiting for.
"And then he asked for a refund." "The nerve of him."
She read the email twice, just to be sure she had it right. "Of all the nerve."
Charging eight dollars for a bottle of water — the nerve.
entries.русский: какая наглость! / ну и наглец — возмущённый приговор, произносимый за глаза
entries.variants: the nerve of him, the nerve of some people, of all the nerve

entries.meaning: A one-word verdict on something outrageous. In the right context it can be admiring, but said flatly about a problem it is pure anger.
examples: "Unbelievable. They towed my car."
Unbelievable — three hours late and not one phone call.
"He denied the whole thing." "Unbelievable."
She looked at the bill. "Absolutely unbelievable."
Unbelievable, I fixed that yesterday and it's already broken.
entries.русский: невероятно! / уму непостижимо — приговор возмутительному; ровным тоном — злость
entries.see also: seriously, are you kidding me, you gotta be kidding me

entries.meaning: An angry question about somebody's judgment, not their health: you are saying that what they did was so thoughtless it needs explaining. Aimed at a stranger it is close to a challenge; aimed at a friend it is a scolding.
examples: "What is wrong with you? That's a fire exit."
What's wrong with you — you cannot say that to a customer.
"He posted the whole conversation online." "What is wrong with people?"
She found the crayon mural in the hallway. "What is wrong with you two?"
Honestly, what is wrong with you, letting the dog drink out of the pool.
entries.русский: ты что, с ума сошёл? / что с тобой не так — упрёк не здоровью, а рассудку
entries.variants: what's wrong with you, what is wrong with people, what the hell is wrong with you
entries.see also: are you kidding me, seriously, honestly

entries.meaning: A stronger, more theatrical are you kidding me, aimed at the universe as much as at any person. It marks the moment something goes wrong on top of something that was already wrong.
examples: "You gotta be kidding me — a second flat tire?"
You've got to be kidding me. The reservation was for tomorrow?
"They lost the paperwork." "You have got to be kidding me."
He watched the elevator doors close in his face. "You gotta be kidding me."
You gotta be kidding me, I just paid that off.
entries.русский: да вы издеваетесь! / этого не может быть — театральнее are you kidding me
entries.variants: you've got to be kidding me, you have got to be kidding me, you gotta be kidding
entries.see also: are you kidding me, unbelievable, seriously

entries.meaning: A flat, sarcastic refusal to be impressed by whatever somebody has just announced. The whoop is a mock cheer, and delivering it without any energy at all is the entire joke.
examples: "Big whoop. I've been doing that job for six years."
"He got a certificate." "Big whoop."
Big whoop — a ten-dollar gift card for working every weekend in December.
She read the employee-of-the-month plaque and muttered, "big whoop."
So he apologized. Big deal. He should never have said it in the first place.
entries.русский: подумаешь! / вот уж радость — саркастический отказ впечатляться
entries.see also: whatever, oh joy, thanks a lot

entries.meaning: A clipped surrender that means the opposite of fine: you are giving in while making sure everyone knows you are unhappy about it. The short, falling fine is one of the most passive-aggressive words in American English.
examples: "Fine. Do it your way."
Fine — I'll drive.
"You have to be there at eight." "Fine."
She grabbed her coat off the hook. "Fine, I'm going."
Fine, don't listen to me.
entries.русский: ну и ладно! / ладно, сквозь зубы — сдача с явным недовольством, пассивная агрессия

entries.meaning: Said flat and falling, the sarcastic opposite of its literal meaning: something has just gone wrong. Learners regularly take this one at face value.
examples: "Great. The car won't start."
Oh great — now it's raining.
"Your flight is delayed four hours." "Great."
He found the milk carton empty in the fridge. "Great."
Great, now I have to do the whole thing over.
entries.русский: ну прекрасно! / замечательно — сказано ровно, значит саркастическое «вот беда»

entries.meaning: Great with the sarcasm made unmistakable by the just. It is almost never sincere.
examples: "Just great. The Wi-Fi is out again."
Oh, just great — I left the tickets at home.
"That's just great, now we're both stuck here."
She read the cancellation notice on the door. "Just great."
Just great, the one day I forget my umbrella.
entries.русский: ну просто замечательно! — тот же сарказм, но уже без всяких сомнений
entries.variants: that's just great, oh just great

entries.meaning: With flat intonation, a sarcastic jab at something clumsy or inconsiderate that somebody just did. With rising intonation the same word is a real compliment, so tone is everything.
examples: "Nice. You just spilled it on the rug."
Nice going — you woke the baby.
"I told her about the party." "Real nice."
He watched the driver take up two spots. "Nice."
Nice one, now the whole file is gone.
entries.русский: ну молодец! / красиво — ровным тоном сарказм; с повышением — настоящая похвала
entries.variants: real nice, nice going, nice one

entries.meaning: Sarcastic delight at something you are dreading. It is drier and more theatrical than great, and it usually introduces the bad news instead of reacting to it.
examples: "Oh joy. Another all-hands meeting."
Oh joy — my in-laws are staying for two weeks.
"You're on the schedule for New Year's Eve." "Oh joy."
He opened the envelope and found a jury summons. "Oh, joy."
Three connecting flights, oh joy, and not one of them on the same airline.
entries.русский: какое счастье! / вот радость-то — сухой сарказм о том, чего вы заранее боитесь
entries.variants: oh joy of joys, what joy

entries.meaning: A sarcastic verdict on a new problem arriving at the worst possible moment. Flat delivery is the only thing marking it as sarcasm.
examples: "Perfect. The printer is out of toner."
Oh perfect — a flat tire on the way to the airport.
"They moved the meeting to Friday at five." "Perfect."
She looked at the coffee stain on her white shirt. "Just perfect."
Perfect, now the neighbors are mowing.
entries.русский: ну просто отлично! / прекрасно — сарказм о новой беде в худший момент

entries.meaning: A mid-century word for excellent that almost nobody uses sincerely anymore, which makes it permanently available for sarcasm. Said flat it works exactly like sarcastic great, with an extra layer of irony from the word itself sounding old.
examples: "Swell. The heat is out and it's twelve degrees."
Oh swell — they gave away our table.
"How's the new job?" "Just swell."
He watched the tow truck pull away with his car. "Swell."
So now I'm paying for both of them. Swell.
entries.русский: чудненько! / расчудесно — устар. «отлично», сегодня почти только с иронией
entries.variants: oh swell, just swell, that's swell

entries.meaning: Another positive word turned sour by flat delivery, a little drier and more dated than sarcastic great. It usually greets news you did not want.
examples: "Terrific. Now we're both late."
Oh terrific — the elevator is broken again.
"They want the report by noon." "Terrific."
He read the notice taped to the door. "Just terrific."
Terrific, the game is blacked out in our area.
entries.русский: великолепно! / чудесно — сарказм, суше и старомоднее, чем great

entries.meaning: Sarcastic thanks for something that made your life harder. Only the flat, clipped delivery separates it from real gratitude.
examples: "Thanks a lot, now I have to redo the whole thing."
Thanks a lot — you told her before I got the chance.
"I ate the last slice." "Thanks a lot."
She wiped the mud off her seat. "Thanks a bunch."
Thanks for nothing, I waited an hour.
entries.русский: спасибо большое! / вот спасибо — саркастическая благодарность за подставу
entries.variants: thanks a bunch, thanks for nothing

entries.meaning: A dismissive surrender that ends a conversation without conceding anything. It reads as rude to most listeners and is the classic teenage response to being corrected.
examples: "Whatever. I'm done arguing about it."
Whatever — do what you want.
"You're the one who forgot." "Yeah, whatever."
He shrugged at the criticism. "Whatever, man."
Whatever, it's not my problem anymore.
entries.русский: да как хочешь / плевать — пренебрежительное закрытие спора, звучит грубовато

entries.meaning: Sarcastic praise for a fresh disaster, a little more formal and a little more bitter than great. The extra syllables give the flat delivery more room to work.
examples: "Wonderful. The dog found the birthday cake."
Oh wonderful — the hotel gave our room away.
"The whole system is down until Monday." "Wonderful."
She found that the leak had reached the carpet. "Just wonderful."
And now the sitter is sick. Wonderful.
entries.русский: чудесно! / великолепно — сарказм о свежей катастрофе, горше и книжнее great
entries.variants: oh wonderful, just wonderful, that's just wonderful
